next.name: MageCart
next.headline: MageCart: card skimmers that hit online shops, from single sites to cloud platforms
next.in_short: MageCart is a name for web card skimming. Attackers plant code on shopping sites to steal card details. Reports describe thousands of sites hit, and attacks on cloud services that serve many stores at once.

sentences.t: MageCart is the name given to a cluster of card-skimming activity, listed in the MISP galaxy catalogue under the name MageCart.
WIRED describes Magecart as a group of hackers whose goal is stealing credit card numbers.
According to WIRED, Magecart has been behind some of the bigger hacks of recent years, from British Airways to Ticketmaster.
Malwarebytes refers to the criminal part of the Magecart cabal, which suggests the name covers more than one party.
WIRED says Magecart hackers cast the widest possible net to find vulnerable ecommerce sites.
Malwarebytes describes compromised shopping sites that were injected with skimmer code.
In the Volusion case, the victim was a provider of cloud-hosted online stores, so the attack reached the stores that rely on it.
Malwarebytes reports that a single line of code added to a shopping site loads a remote piece of JavaScript.
In the Heroku-hosted skimmers it described, a rogue iframe overlays the standard payment form to harvest card data.
The stolen data is sent back in encoded form.
Malwarebytes says threat actors used free Heroku accounts to host their skimmer infrastructure, and that it had earlier documented skimmers served from GitHub and Amazon S3 buckets.
The Volusion report says most Magecart attacks happen when hackers use vulnerabilities in self-hosted stores to plant skimmer code.
The same report describes supply-chain attacks, including seven service providers breached in May 2019 through misconfigured cloud-hosting accounts.
WIRED, in an article published on 2019-07-11, says the group hit 17,000 domains in a few months.
Malwarebytes published a post on 2019-12-03 about skimmers on Heroku. It says the abusive instances were reported to Heroku and taken down.
A report dated Oct. 8, 2019 says hackers breached Volusion and altered a file on its Google Cloud infrastructure so that card details entered in shoppers' forms were captured.
That report says more than 6,500 stores were impacted, that the number could be higher, and that the malicious code was still being delivered at the time of writing.
Shop owners should keep self-hosted store software patched and check the access settings on their cloud-hosting accounts.
Merchants should also review which third-party scripts and providers can touch their payment pages.
